{{Short description|Series representing modular forms}}
{{distinguish|Eisenstein sum}}
{{about|'''holomorphic''' Eisenstein series in dimension 3|the non-holomorphic case|Real analytic Eisenstein series|the higher dimensional case|Siegel Eisenstein series}}
In [[mathematics]], '''Eisenstein series''', named after German mathematician [[Gotthold Eisenstein]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Gotthold Eisenstein - Biography |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Eisenstein/ |access-date=2023-09-05 |website=Maths History |language=en}}</ref> are particular [[modular form]]s with [[infinite series]] expansions that may be written down directly. Originally defined for the [[modular group]], Eisenstein series can be generalized in the theory of [[automorphic form]]s.

== Eisenstein series for the modular group ==
[[Image:Gee_three_real.jpeg|thumb|The real part of {{math|''G''<sub>6</sub>}} as a function of {{mvar|q}} on the [[unit disk]]. Negative numbers are black.]]
[[Image:Gee_three_imag.jpeg|thumb|The imaginary part of {{math|''G''<sub>6</sub>}} as a function of {{mvar|q}} on the unit disk.]]

Let <math>\tau</math> be a [[complex number]] with strictly positive [[imaginary part]]. The '''holomorphic Eisenstein series''' <math>G_{2k}(\tau)</math> of weight <math>2k</math>, where <math>k\geq 2</math> is an [[integer]], is defined by<ref>{{cite journal |last=Gekeler |first=Ernst-Ulrich |date=2011 |title=Para-Eisenstein series for the modular group <math>\operatorname{GL}(2, \mathbb{F}_q[T])</math> |jstor=taiwjmath.15.4.1463 |journal=Taiwanese Journal of Mathematics |volume=15 |issue=4 |pages=1463–1475 |doi=10.11650/twjm/1500406358 |s2cid=119499748 |issn=1027-5487 }}</ref>

:<math>G_{2k}(\tau) = \sum_{(m,n)\in\Z^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}} \frac{1}{(m+n\tau )^{2k}}.</math>

This series [[absolute convergence|absolutely converges]] to a [[holomorphic function]] of <math>\tau</math> in the [[upper half-plane]] and its Fourier expansion given below shows that it extends to a holomorphic function at <math>\tau=i\infty</math>. It is a remarkable fact that the Eisenstein series is a [[modular form]]. Indeed, the key property is its <math>\operatorname{SL}(2,\Z)</math>-invariance. Explicitly, if <math>a,b,c,d</math> are integers and <math>ad-bc=1</math> then

:<math>G_{2k} \left( \frac{a\tau +b}{c\tau + d} \right) = (c\tau +d)^{2k} G_{2k}(\tau)</math>

{{Hidden <!--(omit for initial hidden state)-->
| style = border:1px solid black; text-align:left;width: 70%;
| multiline=
| headerstyle = text-align:left;
| header = (Proof)
| contentstyle = text-align:left;
| content =
:<math>\begin{align}
G_{2k}\left(\frac{a\tau+b}{c\tau+d}\right) &= \sum_{(m,n) \in \Z^2 \setminus \{(0,0)\}} \frac{1}{\left(m+n\frac{a\tau+b}{c\tau+d}\right)^{2k}} \\
&= \sum_{(m,n) \in \Z^2 \setminus \{(0,0)\}} \frac{(c\tau+d)^{2k}}{(md+nb+(mc+na)\tau)^{2k}} \\
&= \sum_{\left(m',n'\right) = (m,n)\begin{pmatrix}d \ \ c\\b \ \ a\end{pmatrix}\atop (m,n)\in \Z^2 \setminus \{(0,0)\}} \frac{(c\tau+d)^{2k}}{\left(m'+n'\tau\right)^{2k}}
\end{align}</math>

If <math>ad-bc=1</math> then
:<math>\begin{pmatrix}d & c\\b & a\end{pmatrix}^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}\ a & -c\\-b & \ d\end{pmatrix}</math>
so that
:<math>(m,n) \mapsto (m,n)\begin{pmatrix}d & c\\b & a\end{pmatrix}</math>
is a bijection <math>\Z^2\to\Z^2</math>, i.e.:
:<math>\sum_{\left(m',n'\right) = (m,n)\begin{pmatrix}d \ \ c\\b \ \ a\end{pmatrix}\atop (m,n)\in \Z^2 \setminus \{(0,0)\}} \frac{1}{\left(m'+n'\tau\right)^{2k}} = \sum_{\left(m',n'\right)\in \mathbb{Z}^2 \setminus \{(0,0)\}} \frac{1}{(m'+n'\tau)^{2k}} = G_{2k}(\tau)</math>

Overall, if <math>ad-bc=1</math> then
:<math>G_{2k}\left(\frac{a\tau+b}{c\tau+d}\right) = (c\tau+d)^{2k} G_{2k}(\tau)</math>

and <math>G_{2k}</math> is therefore a modular form of weight <math>2k</math>.
}}

Note that it is important to assume that <math>k\geq 2</math> to ensure absolute convergence of the series, as otherwise it would be illegitimate to change the order of summation in the proof of <math>\operatorname{SL}(2,\Z)</math>-invariance. In fact, there are no nontrivial modular forms of weight 2. Nevertheless, an analogue of the holomorphic Eisenstein series can be defined even for <math>k=1</math>, although it would only be a [[quasimodular form]]. It is also necessary that the weight be even, as otherwise the sum vanishes because the <math>(-m,-n)</math> and <math>(m,n)</math> terms cancel each other.

== Relation to modular invariants ==
The [[Elliptic modular function|modular invariants]] <math>g_2</math> and <math>g_3</math> of an [[elliptic curve]] are given by the first two Eisenstein series:<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Obers |first1=Niels A. |last2=Pioline |first2=Boris |date=2000 |title=Eisenstein series in string theory |journal=Classical and Quantum Gravity |volume=17 |issue=5 |pages=1215–1224 |doi=10.1088/0264-9381/17/5/330 |issn=0264-9381 |arxiv=hep-th/9910115 |s2cid=250864942 }}</ref>

:<math>\begin{align} g_2 &= 60 G_4 \\ g_3 &= 140 G_6 .\end{align}</math>

The article on modular invariants provides expressions for these two functions in terms of [[theta function]]s.

== Recurrence relation ==
Any holomorphic modular form for the modular group<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mertens |first1=Michael H. |last2=Rolen |first2=Larry |date=2015 |title=Lacunary recurrences for Eisenstein series |journal=Research in Number Theory |volume=1 |article-number=9 |doi=10.1007/s40993-015-0010-x |doi-access=free |arxiv=1504.00356 }}</ref> can be written as a polynomial in <math>G_4</math> and <math>G_6</math>. Specifically, the higher order <math>G_{2k}</math> can be written in terms of <math>G_4</math> and <math>G_6</math> through a [[recurrence relation]]. Let <math>d_k=(2k+3)!G_{2k+4}</math>. Then the <math>d_k</math> satisfy the relation

:<math>\sum_{k=0}^n {n \choose k} d_k d_{n-k} = \frac{2n+9}{3n+6}d_{n+2}</math>

for all <math>n\geq 0</math>.

The <math>d_k</math> occur in the series expansion for [[Weierstrass's elliptic functions]]:

:<math>\begin{align}
\wp(z) &=\frac{1}{z^2} + z^2 \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac {d_k z^{2k}}{k!} \\
&=\frac{1}{z^2} + \sum_{k=1}^\infty (2k+1) G_{2k+2} z^{2k}.
\end{align}</math>

== Fourier series ==
[[Image:Eisenstein_4.jpg|right|thumb|{{math|''G''<sub>4</sub>}}]]
[[Image:Eisenstein_6.jpg|right|thumb|{{math|''G''<sub>6</sub>}}]]
[[Image:Eisenstein_8.jpg|right|thumb|{{math|''G''<sub>8</sub>}}]]
[[Image:Eisenstein_10.jpg|right|thumb|{{math|''G''<sub>10</sub>}}]]
[[Image:Eisenstein_12.jpg|right|thumb|{{math|''G''<sub>12</sub>}}]]
[[Image:Eisenstein_14.jpg|right|thumb|{{math|''G''<sub>14</sub>}}]]

Let <math>q=e^{2\pi i\tau}</math>. Then the [[Fourier series]] of the Eisenstein series is<ref>{{cite journal |last=Karel |first=Martin L. |date=1974 |title=Fourier coefficients of certain Eisenstein series |journal=[[Annals of Mathematics]] |volume=99 |issue=1 |pages=176–202 |doi=10.2307/1971017 |mr=0344195 |zbl=0279.10024}}</ref>

:<math>G_{2k}(\tau) = 2\zeta(2k) \Big(1+c_{2k}\sum_{n=1}^\infty \sigma_{2k-1}(n)q^n\Big).</math>

The coefficients <math>c_{2k}</math> are given by

:<math>c_{2k} = \frac{(2\pi i)^{2k}}{(2k-1)! \zeta(2k)} = \frac {-4k}{B_{2k}} = \frac 2 {\zeta(1-2k)},</math>

where <math>B_n</math> are the [[Bernoulli number]]s, <math>\zeta</math> is the [[Riemann zeta function]] and <math>\sigma_{p}(n)</math> is the [[divisor function|divisor sum function]], i.e. the sum of the <math>p</math>-th powers of the divisors of <math>n</math>. In particular, one has

:<math>G_4(\tau)=\frac{\pi^4}{45} \bigg( 1+ 240\sum_{n=1}^\infty \sigma_3(n) q^{n} \bigg)</math>
and
:<math>G_6(\tau)=\frac{2\pi^6}{945} \bigg( 1- 504\sum_{n=1}^\infty \sigma_5(n) q^n \bigg).</math>

The summation over <math>q</math> can be resummed as a [[Lambert series]]; that is, one has

:<math>\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} q^n \sigma_a(n) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{n^a q^n}{1-q^n}</math>

for arbitrary [[complex number|complex]] <math>|q|<1</math> and <math>a</math>. When working with the [[q-expansion|{{math|''q''}}-expansion]] of the Eisenstein series, this alternate notation is frequently introduced:

:<math>\begin{align}
E_{2k}(\tau)&=\frac{G_{2k}(\tau)}{2\zeta (2k)}\\
&= 1+\frac {2}{\zeta(1-2k)}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{n^{2k-1} q^n}{1-q^n} \\
&= 1- \frac{4k}{B_{2k}}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \sigma_{2k-1}(n)q^n \\
&= 1 - \frac{4k}{B_{2k}} \sum_{d,n \geq 1} n^{2k-1} q^{nd}. \end{align} </math>

== Identities involving Eisenstein series ==

=== Theta functions ===
Given <math>q=e^{2\pi i\tau}</math>, let<ref>{{cite web |title=How to prove this series identity involving Eisenstein series? |url=https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/4284880/how-to-prove-this-series-identity-involving-eisenstein-series |access-date=2023-09-05 |website=Mathematics Stack Exchange |language=en}}</ref>

:<math>\begin{align}
E_4(\tau)&=1+240\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac {n^3q^n}{1-q^n}, \\[5pt]
E_6(\tau)&=1-504\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac {n^5q^n}{1-q^n}, \\[5pt]
E_8(\tau)&=1+480\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac {n^7q^n}{1-q^n},
\end{align}</math>

and define the [[Theta function#Auxiliary functions|Jacobi theta functions]] (which normally use the [[Nome (mathematics)|nome]] <math>e^{\pi i\tau}</math>)

:<math>\begin{align}
a&=\theta_2\left(0; e^{\pi i\tau}\right)=\vartheta_{10}(0; \tau), \\
b&=\theta_3\left(0; e^{\pi i\tau}\right)=\vartheta_{00}(0; \tau), \\
c&=\theta_4\left(0; e^{\pi i\tau}\right)=\vartheta_{01}(0; \tau)
\end{align},</math>

where <math>\theta_m</math> and <math>\vartheta_{ij}</math> are alternative notations. Then we have the symmetric relations

:<math>\begin{align}
E_4(\tau)&= \frac{1}{2}\left(a^8+b^8+c^8\right), \\[5pt]
E_6(\tau)&= \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{\left(a^8+b^8+c^8\right)^3-54(abc)^8}{2}}, \\[5pt]
E_8(\tau)&= \frac{1}{2}\left(a^{16}+b^{16}+c^{16}\right) = a^8b^8 +a^8c^8 +b^8c^8.
\end{align}</math>

Basic algebra immediately implies

:<math>E_4^3-E_6^2 = \frac{27}{4}(abc)^8,</math>

an expression related to the [[J-invariant#Expressions in terms of theta functions|modular discriminant]]

:<math>\Delta = g_2^3-27g_3^2 = (2\pi)^{12}\Big(\frac{abc}{2}\Big)^8</math>

The third [[symmetric relation]] is a consequence of <math>E_8=E_4^2</math> and <math>a^4-b^4+c^4=0</math>.

=== Products of Eisenstein series ===

Eisenstein series form the most explicit examples of [[modular form]]s for the full modular group <math>\operatorname{SL}(2,\Z)</math>. Since the space of modular forms of weight <math>2k</math> has dimension 1 for <math>2k=4,6,8,10,14</math>, different products of Eisenstein series having those weights have to be equal up to a scalar multiple. In fact, we obtain the identities<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Dickson |first1=Martin |last2=Neururer |first2=Michael |date= 2018|title=Products of Eisenstein series and Fourier expansions of modular forms at cusps |journal=[[Journal of Number Theory]] |volume=188 |pages=137–164 |doi=10.1016/j.jnt.2017.12.013|arxiv=1603.00774 |s2cid=119614418 }}</ref>

:<math>E_4^2 = E_8, \quad E_4 E_6 = E_{10}, \quad E_4 E_{10} = E_{14}, \quad E_6 E_8 = E_{14}. </math>

Using the <math>q</math>-expansions of the Eisenstein series given above, they may be restated as identities involving the sums of powers of divisors:

:<math>\bigg(1+240\sum_{n=1}^\infty \sigma_3(n) q^n\bigg)^2 = 1+480\sum_{n=1}^\infty \sigma_7(n) q^n,</math>

hence

:<math>\sigma_7(n)=\sigma_3(n)+120\sum_{m=1}^{n-1}\sigma_3(m)\sigma_3(n-m),</math>

and similarly for the others. The [[theta function]] of an eight-dimensional even [[unimodular lattice]] <math>\Gamma</math> is a modular form of weight 4 for the full modular group, which gives the following identities:

:<math> \theta_\Gamma (\tau)=1+\sum_{n=1}^\infty r_{\Gamma}(2n) q^{n} = E_4(\tau), \qquad r_{\Gamma}(n) = 240\sigma_3(n) </math>

for the number <math>r_\Gamma(n)</math> of vectors of the squared length <math>2n</math> in the  [[E8 lattice|root lattice of the type {{math|''E''<sub>8</sub>}}]].

Similar techniques involving holomorphic Eisenstein series twisted by a [[Dirichlet character]] produce formulas for the number of representations of a [[Natural number|positive integer]] <math>n</math>' as a sum of two, four, or eight squares in terms of the divisors of <math>n</math>.

Using the above recurrence relation, all higher <math>E_{2k}</math> can be expressed as polynomials in <math>E_4</math> and <math>E_6</math>. For example,

:<math>\begin{align}
E_{8} &=   E_4^2 \\
E_{10} &=  E_4\cdot E_6 \\
691 \cdot E_{12} &=  441\cdot E_4^3+    250\cdot E_6^2 \\
E_{14} &= E_4^2\cdot E_6 \\
3617\cdot E_{16} &=  1617\cdot E_4^4+   2000\cdot E_4  \cdot E_6^2 \\
43867 \cdot E_{18} &= 38367\cdot E_4^3\cdot E_6+5500\cdot E_6^3 \\
174611 \cdot E_{20} &= 53361\cdot E_4^5+ 121250\cdot E_4^2\cdot E_6^2 \\
77683 \cdot E_{22} &= 57183\cdot E_4^4\cdot E_6+20500\cdot E_4\cdot E_6^3 \\
236364091 \cdot E_{24} &= 49679091\cdot E_4^6+ 176400000\cdot E_4^3\cdot E_6^2 + 10285000\cdot E_6^4
\end{align}</math>

Many relationships between products of Eisenstein series can be written in an elegant way using [[Hankel matrix|Hankel determinants]], such as Garvan's identity

: <math> \left(\frac{\Delta}{(2\pi)^{12}}\right)^2=-\frac{691}{1728^2\cdot250}\, \begin{vmatrix}E_4&E_6&E_8\\ E_6&E_8&E_{10}\\ E_8&E_{10}&E_{12}\end{vmatrix},</math>

where

:<math> \Delta=(2\pi)^{12}\frac{E_4^3-E_6^2}{1728}</math>

is the [[modular discriminant]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Milne |first=Steven C. |authorlink=Stephen Milne (mathematician) |year=2001 |chapter=Hankel determinants of Eisenstein series |title=Symbolic Computation, Number Theory, Special Functions, Physics and Combinatorics |editor1-last=Garvan |editor1-first=Frank G. |editor2-last=Ismail |editor2-first=Mourad E. H. |publisher=Springer New York |series=Developments in Mathematics |volume=4 |pages=171–188 |doi=10.1007/978-1-4613-0257-5_10}} The paper uses a non-equivalent definition of <math>\Delta</math>, but this has been accounted for in this article.</ref>

=== Ramanujan identities ===
[[Srinivasa Ramanujan]] gave several interesting identities between the first few Eisenstein series involving differentiation.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bhuvan |first1=E. N. |last2=Vasuki |first2=K. R. |date=2019 |title=On a Ramanujan's Eisenstein series identity of level fifteen |journal=Proceedings - Mathematical Sciences |publisher=Indian Academy of Sciences |volume=129 |issue=4 |pages=57 |doi=10.1007/s12044-019-0498-4 |s2cid=255485301 |issn=0973-7685}}</ref> Let

:<math>\begin{align}
L(q)&=1-24\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac {nq^n}{1-q^n}=E_2(\tau), \\[4pt]
M(q)&=1+240\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac {n^3q^n}{1-q^n}=E_4(\tau), \\[4pt]
N(q)&=1-504\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac {n^5q^n}{1-q^n}=E_6(\tau),
\end{align}</math>

then

:<math>\begin{align}
q\frac{dL}{dq} &= \frac {L^2-M}{12}, \\[5pt]
q\frac{dM}{dq} &= \frac {LM-N}{3}, \\[5pt]
q\frac{dN}{dq} &= \frac {LN-M^2}{2}.
\end{align}</math>

These identities, like the identities between the series, yield arithmetical [[convolution]] identities involving the [[divisor function|sum-of-divisor function]]. Following Ramanujan, to put these identities in the simplest form it is necessary to extend the domain of <math>\sigma_p(n)</math> to include zero, by setting
:<math>\sigma_p(0) = \frac{\zeta(-p)}{2}.</math>
Then, for example,

:<math>\sum_{k=0}^n\sigma(k)\sigma(n-k)=\frac{5}{12}\sigma_3(n)-\frac{n\sigma(n)}{2}.</math>

Other identities of this type, but not directly related to the preceding relations between <math>L</math>, <math>M</math> and <math>N</math> functions, have been proved,<ref>{{cite book|authorlink=Srinivasa Ramanujan|last=Ramanujan|first=Srinivasa|chapter=On certain arithmetical functions|pages=136–162|title=Collected Papers|date=1962|publisher=Chelsea|location=New York, NY}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|authorlink=Giuseppe Melfi|first=Giuseppe|last=Melfi|contribution=On some modular identities|title=Number Theory, Diophantine, Computational and Algebraic Aspects: Proceedings of the International Conference held in Eger, Hungary|publisher=Walter de Grutyer & Co.|date=1998|pages=371–382}}</ref> as for example

:<math>\begin{align}
&\sum_{k=0}^n\sigma_3(k)\sigma_3(n-k)=\tfrac1{120}\sigma_7(n), \\[4pt]
&\sum_{k=0}^n\sigma(2k+1)\sigma_3(n-k)=\tfrac1{240}\sigma_5(2n+1), \\[4pt]
&\sum_{k=0}^n\sigma(3k+1)\sigma(3n-3k+1)=\tfrac19\sigma_3(3n+2).
\end{align}</math>

== Generalizations ==
[[Automorphic form]]s generalize the idea of modular forms for general [[semisimple Lie group]]s, where the modular group is replaced by an [[arithmetic group]]. [[Robert Langlands]] generalised the theory of Eisenstein series to this setting.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Moeglin |first1=Colette |last2=Waldspurger |first2=Jean-Loup |title=Spectral Decomposition and Eisenstein Series |series=Cambridge Tracts in Mathematics |volume=113 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |date=1995 |isbn=0-521-41893-3}}</ref>

When the Lie group is of type A<sub>1</sub> the theory resembles the classical case. For example, [[Hilbert modular form]]s are well-studied.
